candidate.title: Context Rot: Agent Accuracy Falls with Session Length, Not Token Count
candidate.abstract: We hold the number of tokens in an agent's context fixed and vary how many turns produced them. Accuracy on follow-up tasks falls by 2 points per 10 turns even when total tokens stay constant, and falls faster when earlier turns contain corrected mistakes. Pruning corrected turns recovers most of the loss.

ranking.why: Separates turn count from token count as the cause of degraded agent context.

candidate.title: Generative AI Policies Across 120 University Syllabi
candidate.abstract: We coded the generative AI policies of 120 syllabi from 14 universities. 41% banned AI outright, 37% allowed it with disclosure and 22% required it for at least one assignment. Courses that required AI also more often redesigned assessment around in-class work.

ranking.why: What university instructors actually allow, ban or require in their AI policies.

candidate.title: Users Edit Agent Plans More Than Agent Outputs
candidate.abstract: In a two-week diary study with 38 knowledge workers using a planning agent, participants edited the agent's plan before execution in 64% of tasks but edited its final output in only 12%. Editing the plan cut the time spent correcting outputs by half.

ranking.why: Where people choose to intervene in agent work, and how much that saves.

candidate.title: Peer Tutoring with LLM Hints in Introductory Physics
candidate.abstract: Pairs of first-year physics students solved problems with or without an LLM that gave hints only to the student acting as tutor. Tutees in the hint condition gained 0.3 standard deviations more on a concept inventory, and tutors gained as much as tutees.

ranking.why: An LLM supporting the student tutor rather than replacing the tutor.
